Section 1 of 14

Does following the Creator guarantee that you will become wealthy?

Some religious speakers make prosperity sound simple:

“Give money, and God will make you rich.”

That message can be especially harmful to people already facing financial pressure. It can turn giving into a transaction and make struggling people feel that poverty proves they lack faith.

That is not the Bible’s message.

The Creator does promise to care for His people. He teaches principles that bring wisdom, freedom, generosity, and peace. But He does not promise that every faithful person will become wealthy.

Jesus lived simply. The apostles faced hardship. Many faithful people in the Bible lost possessions, endured injustice, or died without becoming rich.

Real prosperity is bigger than a bank account. It includes knowing the Creator, having what you truly need, living with integrity, managing resources wisely, helping others, and preparing for eternal life.

Everything belongs to the Creator

Read Psalm 24:1 ↗ and Haggai 2:8 ↗.

The earth, its resources, and every living person belong to the Creator. Human beings may claim property, draw borders, and place their names on legal documents, but they did not create the land.

The Creator also gives us the strength, intelligence, health, opportunities, and relationships that allow us to earn a living.

Read Deuteronomy 8:11–18 ↗.

The Creator warned His people not to look at what they had gained and say, “My power and the might of my hand have gained me this wealth.”

Hard work matters. Education matters. Wise choices matter. But none of us is completely self-made.

Biblical stewardship begins by saying:

“Creator, everything I have comes from You. Show me how to use it well.”

Money is a tool, not a master

Read Matthew 6:19–24 ↗.

Money can provide food, shelter, transportation, education, and help for others. It is not evil.

But money becomes dangerous when it begins controlling our identity and decisions.

Money may promise:

“If you have enough, you will finally be secure.”
“If you buy this, people will respect you.”
“If your income increases, you will become happy.”
“If you cannot afford what others have, you are failing.”

Jesus warned that we cannot serve both God and money. One will eventually take first place.

The Creator does not measure your worth by your income, credit score, job title, clothes, vehicle, or possessions.

You were valuable to Him before you earned your first dollar.

What is tithe?

Read Leviticus 27:30 ↗.

A tithe is one-tenth, or 10 percent, of our income or increase. The Bible calls the tithe holy and says it belongs to the Lord.

That is why believers often speak about “returning” tithe instead of “giving” tithe. We are returning a portion that already belongs to the Creator.

For example:

If your income or increase is $500, the tithe is $50.

If it is $1,000, the tithe is $100.

The amount changes with your income, but the percentage remains the same. This allows people with different incomes to participate by the same principle.

Did tithing begin with ancient Israel?

Read Genesis 14:18–20 ↗ and Genesis 28:20–22 ↗.

Abraham and Jacob practiced tithing long before the nation of Israel was formed at Mount Sinai.

Later, the Creator placed tithing within Israel’s system to support those who devoted their lives to spiritual ministry. Read Numbers 18:21 ↗.

Jesus also spoke about tithing. Read Matthew 23:23 ↗.

He corrected religious leaders because they were careful about tithe while neglecting justice, mercy, and faith. Jesus did not tell them to stop tithing. He said they should practice both.

Returning tithe does not replace compassion. A person cannot mistreat people, ignore injustice, and then use money to appear faithful.

The Creator wants both honesty and love.

What is tithe used for?

Read 1 Corinthians 9:13–14 ↗.

The Bible teaches that those who proclaim the gospel may receive support through the resources God’s people return.

Tithe supports the work of teaching Scripture, caring for congregations, training workers, and carrying the message of Jesus to other communities and nations.

Tithe should be returned through a responsible faith community that handles money openly and uses it for the work the Bible describes.

You have the right to ask reasonable questions about financial accountability. A healthy organization should have clear policies, responsible oversight, accurate records, and protection against one person controlling the money without accountability.

Trust in the Creator does not require ignoring financial warning signs.

Tithe and offerings are different

Read 2 Corinthians 9:6–8 ↗.

Tithe is the 10 percent the Creator identifies as His. Offerings are voluntary gifts given beyond the tithe.

Offerings may support:

  • Local ministry needs
  • Help for struggling families
  • Community service
  • Disaster relief
  • Bible teaching projects
  • Youth programs
  • Mission work
  • Care for elders
  • Other needs the Creator places on your heart

The Bible says giving should not be forced or produced through guilt.

No leader should promise you a miracle in exchange for money. No one should suggest that the Creator will love you more if you give a certain amount.

An offering should come from a willing heart.

What does Malachi’s promise mean?

Read Malachi 3:8–12 ↗.

The Creator told His people they had robbed Him by withholding tithe and offerings. He invited them to return what belonged to Him and trust His provision.

He promised to open the “windows of heaven” and pour out blessing.

This does not mean every faithful giver will receive a larger house, expensive vehicle, or sudden financial success. The Creator’s blessings can take many forms:

  • Daily provision
  • Wisdom to make better decisions
  • Protection from harmful choices
  • Contentment
  • Opportunities to work
  • Help received through community
  • Greater freedom from greed
  • The joy of supporting something eternal
  • Strength during financial hardship

Sometimes the blessing is financial. Sometimes it is not. We should not reduce the Creator’s care to money.

Giving cannot purchase salvation

Read Ephesians 2:8–9 ↗ and Acts 8:18–23 ↗.

Salvation is a gift of grace through Jesus. It cannot be purchased.

Tithe does not pay the Creator for protection. Offerings do not erase sin. Donations do not guarantee that a prayer will be answered in the way we want.

We return tithe because we recognize the Creator’s ownership. We give offerings because His generosity is changing our hearts.

Giving is a response to grace—not the price of grace.

Poverty is not proof of weak faith

Read Luke 21:1–4 ↗ and James 2:1–6 ↗.

Jesus noticed a poor widow who gave two small coins. Her gift mattered because it came from sincere trust, not because it was large.

This story should never be used to pressure struggling people into giving money they do not have. Jesus honored the widow; He did not give religious leaders permission to exploit widows.

A congregation that receives money from people should also care for people in need.

The Bible condemns showing special honor to wealthy people while overlooking those with little. Income does not determine spiritual value.

Some Native communities continue to live with the effects of land loss, broken agreements, limited employment, and economic exploitation. The Bible should never be used to blame people for hardships they did not create.

The Creator sees both personal decisions and unjust systems. He calls individuals to wise stewardship and communities to justice, generosity, and care.

Practice honest work

Read Ephesians 4:28 ↗ and Colossians 3:23–24 ↗.

The Creator values honest work. Your job may not be glamorous or highly paid, but work done with integrity matters to Him.

Work is not only about personal advancement. It also gives us the ability to meet needs and help others.

Avoid income that depends on dishonesty, exploitation, theft, or addiction. No amount of profit can turn wrongdoing into success.

If you are unemployed or unable to work, your value has not decreased. Ask the Creator for direction, take the steps available to you, and allow trustworthy people to help.

Receiving help during a difficult season is not failure.

Plan before spending

Read Luke 14:28–30 ↗.

Jesus spoke about counting the cost before beginning a project. That principle applies to money.

A simple spending plan can help you see where your money is going instead of wondering where it went.

Begin with your actual income. Then list:

  1. Tithe
  2. Basic needs such as housing, food, transportation, and utilities
  3. Required debt payments
  4. Savings when possible
  5. Offerings and help for others
  6. Personal wants

The exact amounts will differ from person to person. The purpose is not to create guilt. It is to make intentional choices.

Even a small amount saved regularly can begin building protection against emergencies.

Be careful with debt

Read Proverbs 22:7 ↗.

Debt can become a form of bondage. Interest charges, payday loans, credit cards, and buy-now-pay-later plans can make a small purchase cost much more than expected.

Not all debt is identical. A reasonable home, education, or business loan may be used carefully. But debt should never be treated like free money.

Before borrowing, ask:

  • Do I truly need this?
  • What will the total cost be?
  • Can I make the payments if my income changes?
  • Am I borrowing because of pressure to impress others?
  • Is there a safer option?

If you already have heavy debt, do not hide in shame. List what you owe, stop adding unnecessary debt, make a repayment plan, and seek trustworthy financial guidance if needed.

The Creator can help you move toward freedom one decision at a time.

Practice contentment

Read Philippians 4:11–13 ↗ and 1 Timothy 6:6–10 ↗.

Paul learned how to live with abundance and with little. His peace did not depend on his circumstances.

Contentment does not mean refusing to improve your situation. You can pursue education, seek better work, build a business, and plan for the future.

Contentment means your happiness is not controlled by comparison.

Social media constantly shows people traveling, buying, achieving, and displaying the best parts of their lives. Comparison can make enough feel like failure.

Ask the Creator to help you enjoy what He has already provided while continuing to grow wisely.

Generosity strengthens community

Read Acts 4:32–35 ↗.

The early believers noticed needs and responded. Those with more helped those with less.

Generosity can include money, but it can also include:

  • Time
  • Food
  • Transportation
  • Skills
  • Encouragement
  • Childcare
  • Mentoring
  • Sharing tools
  • Helping someone find work
  • Listening to a person who feels alone

Strong communities are built when people refuse to live only for themselves.

Generosity should also include wisdom. Helping someone does not always mean giving them everything they request. Love sometimes provides food, treatment, training, accountability, or another form of support instead of cash.

Ask the Creator how to help without enabling harm.

What if you are afraid to return tithe?

You may look at your bills and think:

“I cannot afford to give the Creator the first 10 percent.”

That fear is understandable.

Begin by reviewing your finances honestly. Remove unnecessary expenses where possible. Ask for wisdom. Seek practical guidance. Then decide whether you will trust the Creator with what He has placed in your hands.

Faith does not mean ignoring rent, food, children, or legitimate responsibilities. It means placing the Creator first and allowing His principles to reshape your decisions.

You may not be able to fix every financial problem immediately. Take the next faithful step.

Real prosperity prepares you for eternity

Read Matthew 6:31–33 ↗.

Jesus tells us to seek the Creator’s kingdom first and trust Him with our needs.

You may have much or little. Either way, money will eventually be left behind.

The real question is not:

“How much did I collect?”

It is:

“Did I know the Creator?”
“Did I use what He entrusted to me with integrity?”
“Did my resources help or harm people?”
“Was I faithful?”

Real prosperity means possessing what money cannot buy: forgiveness, purpose, wisdom, healthy relationships, contentment, generosity, and eternal life with Jesus.

Think About It

  1. Do you tend to view money as a tool, a source of identity, or a source of fear?
  2. What does it mean to recognize the Creator as the owner of everything?
  3. How is biblical prosperity different from getting rich?
  4. What concerns do you have about returning tithe?
  5. Is debt, comparison, impulsive spending, or financial secrecy creating stress in your life?
  6. How could your resources strengthen your family or community?

Try This During the Coming Week

Day 1

Read Psalm 24:1 ↗ and Deuteronomy 8:11–18 ↗.

Write down the abilities, opportunities, and resources the Creator has entrusted to you.

Day 2

Read Leviticus 27:30 ↗ and Malachi 3:8–12 ↗.

Calculate 10 percent of your usual income or increase. Ask the Creator to help you understand the principle of returning tithe.

Day 3

Read Matthew 23:23 ↗ and Micah 6:8 ↗.

Consider whether your financial choices reflect justice, mercy, faith, and honesty.

Day 4

Read Luke 14:28–30 ↗.

Create a simple list of your income, expenses, debts, and savings.

Day 5

Read Proverbs 22:7 ↗ and Proverbs 21:20 ↗.

Choose one step that could reduce debt or strengthen your savings.

Day 6

Read 2 Corinthians 9:6–8 ↗.

Choose one voluntary act of generosity. It does not need to be large.

Day 7

Read Matthew 6:25–34 ↗.

Bring your financial fears to the Creator. Ask for daily provision, wisdom, and freedom from comparison.

A Prayer You Can Pray

Creator, everything I have comes from You. Thank You for life, strength, abilities, opportunities, and daily provision.

Forgive me for the times I have allowed money, fear, pride, or comparison to control me.

Teach me to work honestly, spend wisely, avoid harmful debt, save responsibly, return tithe faithfully, and give with a willing heart.

Protect me from people who use Your name to manipulate others for money. Lead me to a faith community that handles resources with honesty and accountability.

Help me trust You when finances are difficult. Give me wisdom to take practical steps and humility to receive help when I need it.

Jesus, teach me to seek Your kingdom first. Give me the kind of prosperity that cannot be lost—faith, peace, integrity, generosity, and eternal life with You. Amen.

Remember This

The Creator does not promise that every faithful person will become wealthy.

Everything belongs to Him, and He asks us to manage what we receive with wisdom and integrity.

Tithe is 10 percent of our income or increase. Offerings are voluntary gifts beyond the tithe.

Giving does not purchase salvation or guarantee luxury. It teaches trust, supports the Creator’s work, helps people, and loosens money’s control over the heart.

Real prosperity is not having everything you want. It is knowing the Creator, having His peace, using resources faithfully, and becoming rich in what lasts forever.
